doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Teaching Steve Allen vibes and conducting for him
summary: Gibbs conducted for Allen for fifteen or sixteen years in clubs and TV, and teaches him vibes.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Oh let me get back to that, because you asked me how I got with Steve. Then Steve asked me if I would conduct for him. And I had another show coming up. By that time I was ready to sit down and settle down. No first he asked me actually if I would go to Las Vegas with him. Because I taught Steve how to play vibes, and we used to close out the show playing the vibes. I taught him how to do that. When he’d come in the club we’d do that. So he thought it’d be good in the show. I would play a song I had written up on “I Got Rhythm,” an arrangement. I played piano with him then I’d play a ballad and show all the technique and everything, and I taught him “Tall Hands” so whatever I did he did just as well. And people thought he was just as good as I was. So we went to Vegas and we closed with that. You know we’d close every show. Then he asked me if I’d like to conduct a television show for him. And so at that time the people who I worked with on Regis Philbin show, a guy called Bill Carruthers, became a big producer/director with Chuck Barris, and they asked me if I would conduct the band for a show called “Operation Entertainment.” And I already was committed. So I did that. And then when I got done with that Steve asked me if I would conduct for him, so I went with Steve and stayed with him for fifteen, sixteen years. We played a lot of night clubs all over the country and television. And he was fun to be with, especially in night clubs, because he’s not like a comedian who tells jokes. If the chandelier fell down, ten more minutes to his act. He looks at anything that goes wrong. In fact when we used to rehearse the band in the afternoon, if a guy came in wearing a weird cap and whatever he was wearing weird, I’d have him wear that cap. I’d have them, whatever weird way they would look, he’d love that. Anything. He’d turn around and look at the band and he’d break up. And he’d work to the band sometimes. He’d turn around and work to the band. We got along real great.
You did a lot of things, for sure.
Yup. It was a big shock for me when he went.
